newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Albania legal system marred by corrupt judges.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Albania legal system marred by corrupt judges.

text.p: Hundreds died in the random trail of devastation left by the armed uprising in Albania. But there was nothing arbitrary about the enraged assaults that destroyed court buildings and prisons across the country.

The new Justice Minister, Spartak Ngjela, understands why the country's 36 courts and seven jails were special targets of hatred in the rebellion that swept across Europe's poorest country in February.

"The people don't trust the courts," said Ngjela, who spent 14 years in jail for criticising Albania's former communist rulers. "I would say about 80 percent of the judges are incompetent. There are judges who cannot even write."

Albania's hopes of restoring law and order rest to no small degree on the shoulders of Ngjela, a straight-talking, self-trained lawyer who took office last month pledging to repair the judicial system -- the cornerstone of any democracy.

"There is no justice in Albania," 49-year-old Ngjela told Reuters. "The mentality is that people don't believe in the justice system. The courts do not have the necessary independence. They are politicised. This is the big defect of Albania."
SEVERAL JAILS DESTROYED
Six of Albania's 36 court buildings were destroyed and five badly damaged in the violence ignited by the collapse of popular, but dubious, investment schemes earlier this year.

The revolt began in the south and quickly spread north. Soldiers and police abandoned their posts. Armouries and police stations were looted and more than a million weapons seized by gangs of bandits and ordinary citizens.
Amid the anarchy, the dilapidated jails were ransacked and more than 1,300 prisoners escaped.

It was an unenviable moment to be named justice minister, especially in a country where there had never been much respect for the law, where courts are widely viewed as corrupt, and where most of the army and half the police force ran away.
But Ngjela was undeterred.

As a former political prisoner, he brought impeccable credentials to the job. After six weeks in the post he is convinced there is a simple cure for many of Albania's otherwise complex problems: build up public confidence in the judiciary.

"The only guarantee for a free society is an independent judiciary," said Ngjela. "Without this, there is no security in your country. If judges are led by politicians, there will be no justice for Albanians."

The U.S. State Department had also issued warnings about Albanian courts. In a report on human rights for 1996, it said that one of the main problems facing Albania was that it has "a judiciary that is subject to widespread corruption and executive pressure and lacking in resources, training and experience."
NO BITTERNESS ABOUT LONG JAIL TERM

Ngjela is a small robust man with thick white hair. He shows no bitterness over the 14 years he spent in jail, locked up in the notorious Burrel prison in 1976 for making critical remarks about communist dictator Enver Hoxha.
While in jail he studied law "and tried to avoid delerium." Ngjela also taught himself to read English, Italian and French.
A broad smile flashes across his face when asked if he ever dreamed while in prison of someday becoming justice minister.
"Could you ever imagine that the communist system would end?" he replied. "That was the most incomprehensible thing for me. I thought if that ever happened, anything was possible."

Ngjela's first act after being appointed on March 13 was to set up special police units to confront and disarm gunmen. He offered officers 30 times their average wage, up to $100 a day in a country where most earn less than that each month. Ngjela and other ministers earn $400 a month.
In another move underlining his determination to establish law and order, he stationed armoured personnel carriers (APCs) in front of the first courts to reopen in early April.

Ngjela also offered an amnesty to escaped prisoners. Those who returned voluntarily to jail by April 12 got one-third off their sentences, a move that effectively pardoned more than 600 convicts. But only about 80 of some 700 still at large returned.
EFFORTS TO FREE JUDGES FROM POLITICAL INTERFERENCE
Ngjela is now focusing his efforts on freeing the country's 200 judges from political interference.

He has drafted legislation that he hopes will quickly win government and parliamentary approval. Judges would no longer be appointed by the Supreme Judicial Council, which is headed by President Sali Berisha and has broad powers to appoint, discipline, demote and fire them.

Seventeen judges were removed in 1996 -- for falsifying documents, giving out light sentences for serious crimes, and taking bribes. But the U.S. State Department report said the selection of replacements was based on ties to Berisha's party.

"Many lawyers report that loyalty to the ruling Democratic party is the key prerequisite in selecting their replacements," the report said. "Judges' salaries are low and there are widespread accusations of corruption."
Even Ngjela's predecessor, Kristofor Peci, said before the uprising that corruption was a "virus" that had infected the courts.

The main opposition Socialist party, now sharing power in the emergency all-party government, has long accused Berisha of perverting the course of justice. Many judges were appointed after just six months' legal training.
"I want to repair the appointment process," said Ngjela. "I want to guarantee the independence of the judges. If people see the courts are independent, they will start trusting them."
NEED TO FIGHT CORRUPTION IN JUDICIARY

Ngjela said it was impossible to talk about "restoring faith" in Albanian justice because none ever existed in the thoroughly corrupt system that flourished under the communists and the first post-communist governments.
"If a politician says 'punish this person', the judge would do it," Ngjela said. "I want to set up new structures and institutions that will prevent this."

One Tirana lawyer said the reforms could help a system in dire need of repair. "I doubt this will happen any time soon," she said. "I doubt corruption will be crushed so easily. It will remain a serious threat especially because there is so much poverty and judges can so easily be bought."
Ngjela wants to pay judges far more than they currently earn -- about $150 to $300 a month.

Despite their modest salaries, many judges manage to buy enormous villas worth more than $100,000 in Tirana's leafy outskirts. Their palatial residences often come up in conversations about justice with Albanians.
"You pay, you win," said one Tirana man. "If you want to win your case, everyone knows you need money."

A Tirana businessman said people had grown sceptical after seeing suspected criminals walking around town shortly after they were shown on television being arrested for serious crimes. "Everyone assumes a judge was paid some money," he said. "No one I know trusts them."
